reason: Sunlight can power evaporation from the sea, beginning the return of fresh water.
expectation: Solar heating will produce water vapor from the sea.

effect: Evaporation has moved water into the air while leaving most dissolved minerals behind; cooling it is the next step toward fresh water.
reaction: The distinction between evaporating water and the minerals left behind is satisfying.
reason: Cool air should condense the evaporated water into clouds.

choice.with: Cooler air high above the surface

expectation: Water vapor will condense into cloud droplets.

effect: The evaporated water has condensed into a cloud, ready to move toward the shore.
reaction: The contrast between seawater and the resulting cloud is clear.
reason: Wind could carry the cloud toward land, continuing the water cycle.
expectation: The wind will move the cloud toward the shore.

effect: The cloud has moved over land, bringing sea-derived moisture closer to the shore.
reaction: The water cycle is progressing as expected.
reason: The rocky rise may lift the moist cloud and encourage rain.

choice.with: A rocky rise behind the shore

expectation: Air rising over the rocky ground will cool and produce rain.

effect: The cloud produced rain on the rise; the slope may now carry that fresh water back toward the shore.
reaction: The rising-air explanation makes the rainfall mechanism clear.
reason: Water falling on the rocky rise can run downhill toward the basin and shore.

choice.with: A slope toward a broad basin

expectation: Rainwater will flow down the slope toward the shore.

effect: The stream completes the fresh-water goal; moonlight remains to be made visible on the water. The sea is no longer selectable.
reaction: It is satisfying to see the water return to the sea.
reason: The Moon and the remaining tidal pools are a plausible pair for the moonlight goal, though the exact combination is a guess.

choice.combine: The Moon with a pale early crust
choice.with: Pools left behind by the tide

expectation: Moonlight will appear in the tidal pools.

effect: The Moon has no available combination, so I need another route to the moonlight goal.
reaction: I’m surprised the Moon cannot be used directly.
reason: Easing wind could leave the tidal pools still enough to reflect moonlight.

choice.combine: Pools left behind by the tide

expectation: The pools will become still and show moonlight.

choice.inspect: Pools left behind by the tide

alternatives.reason: I could check their available partners instead of guessing.

effect: The easing wind made a still pool at night, providing a surface for the remaining moonlight goal.
reaction: The quiet pool is a fitting contrast to the moving sea.
reason: The still pool may now be able to reflect the Moon, even though the earlier pool could not combine with it.

choice.with: The Moon with a pale early crust

expectation: The Moon will be reflected in the still pool.

effect: The still pool reflected the Moon and completed the remaining goal; calm water makes the image steadier.
reaction: The reflected sunlight linking Moon and pool is a satisfying ending.

mostWorthwhile.text: Making rain on the rocky rise was worthwhile: it connected wind transport, rising air and cooling to rainfall.

leastWorthwhile.text: The direct Moon-and-pool attempt was least worthwhile because it produced no useful compatibility information beyond the Moon having no available combination.

surprise.text: I was surprised that the Moon could not combine with the tidal pools until the water was made still.

arbitrary.text: Having to make the pool still before using the Moon initially felt arbitrary, although the final explanation makes the clearer reflection understandable.

continue.text: I would choose to continue if another chapter offered similarly concrete natural processes to explore; the water cycle and reflection made this chapter's connections clear.
